newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Riga airport sees cargo trade up 5-10 pct in '97.
newsitem.headline: Riga airport sees cargo trade up 5-10 pct in '97.

text.p: Riga International Airport (RIA) said on Friday it expects its cargo business to rise as much as 10 percent this year on the strength of growing traffic to Britain and the former Soviet Union.
"My expectation is that exports could increase five percent, even 10 percent, from last year," Indulis Blums, RIA's senior cargo agent, told Reuters.
"I expect the same to hold for imports. We are paying more attention to develop our cargo business," Blums said, noting that RIA also acts as a cargo sales agent for several airlines.

These airlines include Austrian Airlines, Czech national carrier Ceske Aerolinie AS (CSA), Polish national carrier PLL LOT SA, German regional airline Hamburg Airlines and Scandinavian Airline Systems (SAS), he said.
The airport's cargo trade, including exports and imports, has been fairly steady in recent years, totalling 3,912 tonnes in 1996, 3,918 tonnes in 1995 and 3,899 tonnes in 1994, Blums said.
The greatest growth will come on routes to Britain, led by British Airways Plc, which on March 30 started flying four times a week between London-Gatwick airport and RIA, Blums said.
Riga Airlines already flies four times a week to Gatwick, he added.

"Cargo growth should be strongest with London because of the new British Airways flights," he said. "Riga Airlines also expects good cargo growth on its flight because it can carry goods from Britain onto Moscow."
Main cargo exports to Britain include computer and electronic parts as well as pharmaceuticals, Blums said.
Air cargo to the former Soviet Union also is growing, especially to the capitals of two central Asian states -- Almaty in Kazakhstan and Tashkent in Uzbekistan, Blums said.
Traffic to Russia also will grow if Latvia's national airline Air Baltic succeeds in starting flights to Moscow and St Petersburg, he said.
"Demand for flights to the former Soviet Union is increasing, because Latvian exporters have started to find markets there," Blums said.
"A lot of business documentation travels on these flights because Latvian companies are changing the nature of their relationship with other countries in the former Soviet Union."
Another big export destination has been Tel Aviv, he said.
"Leather bags and clothing from Latvia are popular there, and a lot of personal items are sent because of immigration to Israel," he said.
